title: Antiderivatives & the Fundamental Theorem
summary: The definite integral $\int_a^b f\,dx$ is the net signed area under $f$. The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus evaluates it as $F(b)-F(a)$ for any antiderivative $F$, and says $\frac{d}{dx}\int_a^x f\,dt=f(x)$ — integration and differentiation are inverses.

antiderivative.plain: A function whose derivative is the integrand.

definite integral.plain: Net signed area between a curve and the axis on $[a,b]$.
definite integral.in_class: $\int_a^b f\,dx$; a number, not a family.

Fundamental Theorem Part 1.plain: The derivative of an accumulation function is the integrand.

Fundamental Theorem Part 2.plain: Evaluate a definite integral with any antiderivative.

net area.plain: Area above the axis minus area below it.
net area.in_class: The definite integral counts below-axis regions as negative.

average value.plain: The mean height of a function over an interval.

concept_sections.heading: Antiderivatives review
concept_sections.explanation: Reverse the derivative rules: $\int x^n\,dx=\dfrac{x^{n+1}}{n+1}+C$, $\int e^x\,dx=e^x+C$, $\int\frac1x\,dx=\ln|x|+C$, and the trig reversals. The $+C$ captures all antiderivatives.
math_steps: Recall which derivative gives the integrand.

concept_sections.heading: The definite integral as net area
concept_sections.explanation: $\int_a^b f\,dx$ is the limit of Riemann sums — the net area, with area below the axis subtracted. Linearity and the endpoint-swap rule ($\int_a^b=-\int_b^a$) simplify computations.
math_steps: Interpret the integral as signed area.
Swap limits with a sign change if needed.

figure.caption: The definite integral as net area

concept_sections.heading: FTC Part 2: evaluating
concept_sections.explanation: To compute $\int_a^b f\,dx$, find any antiderivative $F$ and subtract: $F(b)-F(a)$. This turns an area (a limit of sums) into one subtraction.

concept_sections.heading: FTC Part 1: accumulation
concept_sections.explanation: The area accumulated from $a$ to $x$ defines $A(x)=\int_a^x f\,dt$, and $A'(x)=f(x)$. Differentiation undoes the accumulation — with the chain rule when the upper limit is a function.
math_steps: Its derivative is the integrand at the top limit.
Apply the chain rule if the top limit is $g(x)$.

concept_sections.heading: Average value
concept_sections.explanation: The average value of $f$ on $[a,b]$ is $\dfrac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f\,dx$ — the constant height with the same area. The Mean Value Theorem for integrals guarantees $f$ actually attains it.

real_world_examples.title: Total distance from a speedometer
real_world_examples.scenario: A car's speed is logged over a trip.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Integrating speed over time gives total distance — FTC Part 2 with velocity as the integrand.

real_world_examples.title: Accumulated interest
real_world_examples.scenario: Interest accrues continuously at a varying rate.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The accumulation function $\int_0^t r(s)\,ds$ totals the interest, and its derivative recovers the instantaneous rate.

real_world_examples.title: Average temperature
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: The average value integral gives the day's mean temperature.
